grammar_rules.rule_name: Conjugation of regular -er verbs in present tense
grammar_rules.summary: To conjugate a regular -er verb in the present, remove the -er ending to find the root, then add the endings -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent.
grammar_rules.explanation: Regular -er verbs follow a consistent pattern: the root is obtained by removing -er from the infinitive. The endings are added according to the subject pronoun. The -e, -es, and -ent endings are silent. Liaison occurs between the final -s of nous, vous, ils, elles and a following vowel sound, producing a z sound.
grammar_rules.formation: root + ending: je -e, tu -es, il/elle/on -e, nous -ons, vous -ez, ils/elles -ent
usage: To express actions in the present tense
conditions: Verb must be a regular -er verb
common_traps: Liaison after nous, vous, ils, elles

study.frequency_note: Very high frequency; foundational for French grammar.

attestations.source_text: The endings for the -er regular verbs are: -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent.

grammar_rules.summary: In verbs ending in -cer, the c changes to ç before the letter o to keep the soft pronunciation.
grammar_rules.explanation: The cedilla (ç) is added to c before o in the nous form to preserve the /s/ sound.
common_traps: Forgetting to add cedilla before o

attestations.source_text: the -c- becomes -ç- before the letter o. The cedilla (ç) under the c is needed to keep the soft pronunciation.

grammar_rules.summary: In verbs ending in -ger, the g becomes ge before the letter o to keep the soft pronunciation.
grammar_rules.explanation: The e is added after g before o in the nous form to preserve the /ʒ/ sound.
common_traps: Forgetting to add e after g before o

attestations.source_text: the -g- becomes -ge- before the letter o.

grammar_rules.summary: Verbs like acheter add an accent grave (è) in all forms except nous and vous.
grammar_rules.explanation: The silent e becomes è in the stem for je, tu, il/elle/on, ils/elles to maintain pronunciation.
grammar_rules.formation: j'achète, tu achètes, il/elle achète, ils/elles achètent; nous achetons, vous achetez
usage: Present tense, all persons except first and second plural
common_traps: Adding accent in nous/vous forms incorrectly

attestations.source_text: An accent grave is added in all but the first- and the second-person plural.

grammar_rules.summary: Verbs like répéter change é to è in all forms except nous and vous.
grammar_rules.explanation: The acute accent (é) becomes grave accent (è) in the stem for je, tu, il/elle/on, ils/elles.
grammar_rules.formation: je répète, tu répètes, il/elle répète, ils/elles répètent; nous répétons, vous répétez
usage: Present tense, all persons except first and second plural

attestations.source_text: The é aigu changes to an è grave in all but the first- and second-person plural.

grammar_rules.summary: Verbs like épeler double the l in all forms except nous and vous.
grammar_rules.explanation: The consonant l is doubled in je, tu, il/elle/on, ils/elles forms.
grammar_rules.formation: j'épelle, tu épelles, il/elle épelle, ils/elles épellent; nous épelons, vous épelez
usage: Present tense, all persons except first and second plural

attestations.source_text: sometimes take two ls in all but the first- and second-person plural.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Present tense for general statements and ongoing actions
grammar_rules.summary: The present indicative can express general truths and actions happening now, translatable as simple present, present progressive, or emphatic present.
grammar_rules.explanation: The same French present tense corresponds to three English forms: simple present, present progressive, and emphatic present.
transformations: Can be translated as 'is doing', 'does', or 'does do'

attestations.section_title: When is the present tense used in French?
attestations.source_text: To make a general statement and to describe ongoing actions in the present. It can be translated in three different ways.

grammar_rules.summary: The present tense can be used to express a near future event.
grammar_rules.explanation: Often used with time expressions indicating future, like demain soir.
grammar_rules.formation: Present tense verb + future time expression
restrictions: Usually with explicit future time reference

attestations.section_title: When is the present tense used in French?

grammar_rules.summary: The present tense expresses habitual or repeated actions.
grammar_rules.explanation: Often accompanied by adverbs of frequency or time expressions like tous les jours, d'habitude.

attestations.section_title: When is the present tense used in French?

grammar_rules.rule_name: Present tense for past action connected to present
grammar_rules.summary: The present tense can describe a past action that has immediate relevance or consequence in the present.
grammar_rules.explanation: Often used with verbs like revenir, rentrer, and expressions like à peine.
conditions: Action just completed or still relevant

attestations.section_title: When is the present tense used in French?
attestations.source_text: To describe a past action closely connected to the present

grammar_rules.summary: The present tense can narrate historical events for immediacy.
grammar_rules.explanation: Common in journalistic or literary style.

attestations.section_title: When is the present tense used in French?

grammar_rules.summary: The present tense can describe past events dramatically.
grammar_rules.explanation: Used to make narrative more vivid.

grammar_rules.summary: To express an action in progress, use être en train de + infinitive.
grammar_rules.explanation: This construction emphasizes the ongoing nature of the action.
grammar_rules.formation: conjugated être + en train de + infinitive
grammar_rules.word_order: subject + être + en train de + infinitive
grammar_rules.affirmative_form: je suis en train de parler

attestations.section_title: When is the present tense used in French?
attestations.source_text: To express an action in the process, être en train de + the infinitive form of the verb is used.

grammar_rules.summary: Use the present tense with depuis to express an action that started in the past and continues in the present.
grammar_rules.explanation: In English, the past tense or present perfect is often used, but French uses present tense. Questions can be formed with depuis quand, depuis combien de temps, il y a... que, ça fait... que.
grammar_rules.word_order: depuis can be placed before or after the clause
grammar_rules.interrogative_form: depuis quand, depuis combien de temps, il y a combien de temps que, ça fait combien de temps que
common_traps: Using past tense instead of present

attestations.source_text: EXERCICE 1·10 Traduire les phrases suivantes en utilisant vous et l’inversion si nécessaire.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Silent endings in -er verbs
exceptions_and_traps.description: The -e, -es, and -ent endings of regular -er verbs are silent in pronunciation.

attestations.source_text: The -e, -es, and -ent endings of the verbs are all silent.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Liaison after plural subject pronouns
exceptions_and_traps.description: The final -s of nous, vous, ils, elles links with a following vowel sound, making a z sound.

attestations.source_text: The final -s of nous, vous, ils, elles links with verbs beginning with a vowel sound, making a z sound.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Tu vs vous
exceptions_and_traps.description: Use tu for friends, family, children, animals. Use vous for strangers, people you don't know well, or to maintain distance/respect.

attestations.source_text: Use tu to talk to friends, family members, children, and animals. Use vous when you are addressing a stranger, someone you don't know well, or to maintain a certain degree of distance or respect.

exceptions_and_traps.title: On as impersonal pronoun
exceptions_and_traps.description: The pronoun on can mean one, we, or they depending on context.

attestations.source_text: The pronoun on takes on different meanings. It may mean one, we, or they depending on how it is used.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Using present tense with depuis vs English
exceptions_and_traps.description: In English, past tense or present perfect is often used, but French uses present tense with depuis.

attestations.section_title: One more use of the present tense: depuis
attestations.source_text: Note that in English, the past tense is used.
